documents.title: Guidelines for Using Generative AI
documents.stance_why: The guidelines set no course-level rule; they hand AI expectations to faculty ('communicate clear expectations') and add general duties on data protection, tool review, responsibility for output and disclosure. No tiers or permit/prohibit rule is given.
documents.summary: University-wide guidelines (Sept 2026) for students, faculty and staff on generative AI: work within existing policies and the Honor Code, protect data and use only reviewed tools, own and verify output, and disclose use. Faculty are asked to set expectations in courses.

units.why: The guidelines promise revision: 'we will update these guidelines as the field progresses', so this is a statement that the policy is provisional, which is the revisit-regularly type.
units.anchor: we will update these guidelines as the field progresses

units.why: Opening scope statement that the guidelines set ethical considerations for 'students, faculty, and staff'; an institution-wide framework preamble, so P56 not P61 since it defines no terms.
units.anchor: ethical considerations and guidelines for the use of Generative AI

units.why: Requires AI use to be 'consistent with existing University policies' (named technology, data classification and data management policies); this is the comply-with-existing-policy type.
units.anchor: Use AI tools consistent with existing University policies

units.why: 'Students must abide by the Honor Code' puts students under existing integrity rules without stating that AI misuse is misconduct, so P77 (comply with existing policy) rather than P36.
units.anchor: Students must abide by the Honor Code.
units.fit_note: Honor Code is an academic-integrity code, so it also shades toward P36, but the text never names AI misuse as a violation.

units.why: Faculty 'are asked to... communicate clear expectations to students on using generative AI in their courses', a duty to state AI expectations; modality should because it is phrased as a request.
units.anchor: communicate clear expectations to students on using generative AI in their courses
units.fit_note: Does not say the expectations must be in the syllabus; the place is left open.

units.why: Faculty are directed to read OTL resources on AI in the classroom, a pointer that supports faculty learning about AI before setting course policy.
units.anchor: read the Office of Teaching and Learning’s resources about

units.why: 'Entering information into AI tools is similar to posting that information on a public website' is a warning about data privacy, an informing statement under protect-personal-data.
units.anchor: Entering information into AI tools is similar to posting that information on a public website.

units.why: Explains that data entered 'could become part of its training data' and be reproduced to outsiders; a privacy and confidentiality fact supporting the data-protection rule.
units.anchor: Any data entered into such tools could become part of its training data

units.why: Limits use of University information with AI to public data or reviewed tools with contract terms; its core is tool review and approval (P65) though it also protects data (P50), and P65 names review before use.
units.anchor: may use University information with generative AI tools or services only when
units.frag_start: Faculty, students, and staff may use
units.fit_note: Also a data-protection rule: only public information may go into unreviewed tools.

units.why: 'If you aren't sure, contact the IT help center' tells users to ask before using a tool with University information; closest is P10, but it asks IT rather than the instructor.
units.anchor: If you aren’t sure, contact the IT help center
units.fit_note: Directs people to IT staff about tool review, not to the instructor about whether AI is allowed in a course.

units.why: Tells users to review vendor usage policies 'regularly' because they change without notice; this is about staying current with external terms, nearest P102 though it names terms of service not AI developments.
units.anchor: These policies are frequently updated without notice and should be reviewed regularly.
units.fit_note: Concerns vendor terms of service and lawful use, not general AI developments or the university's guidance.

units.why: 'Adhere to ethical and legal standards and norms of the disciplines and the University' sets a general duty to comply with laws and norms (privacy, consent, ownership, integrity), so P77.
units.anchor: Adhere to ethical and legal standards and norms of the disciplines and the University
units.fit_note: Also lists integrity, privacy, consent and ownership as ethical concerns.

units.why: 'You are 100% responsible for the output you use' makes users own what they use from AI, the own-everything-you-submit type.
units.anchor: You are 100% responsible for the output you use.

units.why: Warns output may be 'biased, inaccurate, completely fabricated' and requires 'thorough human review prior to use'; verify-AI-output type.
units.anchor: therefore requiring thorough human review prior to use

units.why: Notes output may 'contain copyright-protected or proprietary information', a licensing and IP concern about AI output.
units.anchor: contain copyright-protected or proprietary information

units.why: 'Be transparent and cite usage of AI... clearly documented and disclosed' requires disclosure for DU work and research, the disclose-with-submission type.
units.anchor: should be clearly documented and disclosed
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI for any
units.fit_note: Scope is 'research, scholarship or work', not specifically course submissions; no format for the citation is given.

units.why: 'When in doubt, reach out' tells people to seek help (IT staff) for use cases and risks; asking-before-use type, with a note it routes to IT.
units.anchor: When in doubt, reach out.
units.fit_note: Routes to IT staff to explore use cases and mitigate risks, not to the instructor.

documents.title: Concerns About Student Use (Artificial Intelligence)
documents.stance_why: The page advises faculty ('Consider syllabus statements indicating whether and how AI tools can be used') and says responses depend on 'your course and/or department/program policies'; it fixes no stance and offers no tiers.
documents.summary: Teaching-center advice for faculty worried about student AI use: discuss integrity early, state syllabus expectations, design assessments to be hard to outsource, and handle suspicion by conversation rather than detector software. Includes input from the Writing Center, Career office and a college's AI tutorials.

units.why: States the page's aim: AI use should enhance 'rather than detracts from' education, a purpose statement for the guidance.
units.anchor: ensuring that its use enhances, rather than detracts from, the educational experience
units.fit_note: Purpose statement for a guidance page rather than an institution-wide framework.

units.why: Faculty are to 'carve out time for robust discussions about academic honesty' at the quarter's start, an instruction to explain and discuss integrity expectations with students.
units.anchor: carve out time for robust discussions about academic honesty, integrity, and ethics
units.frag_start: At the beginning of the quarter

units.why: Faculty should 'make sure they are familiar with the University of Denver Honor Code'; points students to the integrity code and is about explaining rules, nearest P66.
units.anchor: Make sure they are familiar with the
units.fit_note: About familiarity with the Honor Code in general, not AI rules specifically.

units.why: 'Be very clear about your expectations' and consider syllabus statements on whether and how AI can be used; advises putting AI expectations in the syllabus, though only 'consider'.
units.anchor: Consider syllabus statements indicating whether and how AI tools can be used.
units.fit_note: Syllabus statement is suggested ('consider'), not required.

units.why: Offers sample policies and 'local examples' and invites faculty to share their own; resources to help instructors write course policy, closest to supporting faculty.
units.anchor: We’ve added a section to our

units.policy: OTL has added a section on AI tools with local examples to its Sample Syllabus Statements page, and faculty may email their own statements to otl@du.edu.
units.fit_note: Sample statements and sharing, not workshops or consultations.

units.why: Advises assessing 'throughout the course' with formative approaches rather than only a final project, a redesign of assessment in response to AI concerns.
units.anchor: assess student learning throughout the course

units.why: Suggests learning students' writing styles via an early reflection and low-stakes writing so staff can spot work that is not theirs; process evidence for identifying misuse, nearest P40.
units.anchor: get to know your students’ writing styles
units.frag_start: As much as is possible given class size
units.fit_note: Builds a baseline of student writing rather than using software or commit logs.

units.why: Advises specific prompts that require synthesis because 'ChatGPT struggles with details and making connections'; assignment design to resist AI.
units.anchor: Write specific prompts that asks students to synthesize knowledge

units.why: 'Don't rely on AI checking software to confirm your suspicions' calls detectors unreliable and not to be relied on.
units.anchor: Don’t rely on AI checking software to confirm your suspicions.

units.why: Tells instructors not to assume 'the worst and demonizing the student', a call for a fair, good-faith response rather than punishment first.
units.anchor: Instead of assuming the worst and demonizing the student
units.fit_note: Chosen over P57 for the good-faith framing; the conversation itself is coded next.

units.why: Suggests asking the student about their writing process, e.g. in office hours, before asking about AI; talking with the student before escalating.
units.anchor: Ask the student about their writing process
units.frag_start: If AI tools are banned in your class

units.why: After the conversation the instructor 'can decide how to proceed based on your course and/or department/program policies', leaving response to course and department rules.
units.anchor: you can decide how to proceed based on your course and/or department/program policies
units.frag_start: Depending on how the student responds
units.fit_note: Applies to handling suspected misuse, not to whether AI is permitted.
